specPoints.text: calculate relative formula masses (including relative molecular masses) (Mr) from relative atomic masses (Ar)

primer.text: The Periodic Table gave you a relative atomic mass for every element - the larger of the two numbers beside each symbol. This note builds compounds from that starting point: the relative formula mass totals the atomic masses of every atom a formula contains, brackets included. It is the number every reacting-mass working later in this subtopic rests on, so the adding has to be exact.

lessons.title: Relative Atomic Mass and Relative Formula Mass
sourceHeadings: Relative Formula Mass & Relative Molecular Mass
lessons.opening: Every element carries a relative atomic mass, Ar, printed on the Periodic Table as the larger of its two numbers. A compound has no atomic mass of its own, so it borrows one: the relative formula mass, Mr, totals the atomic masses of all the atoms its formula contains. Add the Ar value of each atom present, and the total is the Mr you can take into any later working.
keyPoints: The relative atomic mass (Ar) of an element is the larger of the two numbers beside its symbol on the Periodic Table.
The relative formula mass (Mr) of a substance is the total of the atomic masses of every atom its formula contains.
Mr is also called the relative molecular mass when the substance is a simple molecule.
Conservation of mass means the total relative formula mass of the reactants equals that of the products in a balanced equation.
Ar values come from the mass number and the relative abundances of an element's isotopes.

low.restatement: Find Ar on the Periodic Table, then add one Ar for every atom the formula shows: water, H2O, reads (2 x 1) + (1 x 16) = 18, and hydrogen gas, H2, reads 2 x 1 = 2.
low.analogy: Treat it like a shopping bill: each element has a fixed price tag (its Ar), the subscript tells you how many of that item you are buying, and Mr is simply the bill for one formula.
low.examPointer: The larger of the two numbers beside a symbol is Ar; quote it from the table before you add anything, and keep 35.5 for chlorine exactly as printed.

medium.restatement: Relative masses compare atoms against a standard, so they are plain numbers with no units; adding them for a formula gives Mr, which is why a water molecule totals 18 from two hydrogens at 1 and one oxygen at 16.
medium.analogy: Think of a recipe card: hydrogen and oxygen each carry a fixed unit cost, and one serving of H2O costs two hydrogen units plus one oxygen unit - 18 in all.
medium.examPointer: If asked why Mr carries no unit, say the masses are relative comparisons rather than gram masses, so no unit attaches to either Ar or Mr.

check.stem: Which number on the Periodic Table is an element's relative atomic mass?

options.text: The larger of the two numbers beside the symbol
options.explanation: Ar sits beside the symbol as the larger number; the smaller one is the atomic number.

options.text: The smaller of the two numbers beside the symbol
options.explanation: That smaller number is the atomic number, which counts protons and never gives the mass.

options.text: The charge on its ion
options.explanation: Ion charges describe electron loss or gain, not the mass of the atom.

options.text: The number of the period it sits in
options.explanation: The period number counts occupied shells; it carries no mass value.

check.stem: What does the relative formula mass, Mr, of a substance describe?

options.text: The total mass of all the atoms present in one formula
options.explanation: Mr adds one Ar for every atom the formula contains, giving the formula's total relative mass.

options.text: The mass of a single atom of the element
options.explanation: That value is Ar, which belongs to one atom; Mr belongs to the whole formula.

options.text: The number of atoms in the formula
options.explanation: Mr is a mass total, not a count; the subscripts give the count and the Ar values give the mass.

options.text: The mass of one mole of the substance in grams
options.explanation: A mass in grams per mole is a later idea; Mr itself is a unit-free relative total.

check.stem: Using Ar values H = 1 and O = 16, what is the relative formula mass of water, H2O?

options.explanation: (2 x 1) + (1 x 16) = 18, so a water molecule totals 18.
This forgets to double the hydrogen: two H atoms contribute 2, not 1.
This drops the hydrogen entirely; both elements in the formula must be counted.
This doubles the oxygen as well as the hydrogen; the subscript 2 belongs to H only.

check.stem: A molecule of hydrogen gas is H2. Using Ar H = 1, what is its relative formula mass?

options.explanation: Two hydrogen atoms each contribute 1, so the formula mass is 2 x 1 = 2.
This counts one atom only; the subscript shows hydrogen gas travels as a pair.
Dividing instead of multiplying has no meaning here; each atom adds its Ar once.

options.text: There is no Mr for an element
options.explanation: Elements that form molecules still have formula masses; H2 is a molecule of two atoms.

check.stem: In a balanced equation, how does the total relative formula mass of the reactants compare with that of the products?

options.text: They are equal, because mass is conserved
options.explanation: The law of conservation of mass fixes the totals on both sides of the equation.

options.text: The products total more, because new material is made
options.explanation: No new material appears in a chemical reaction; mass is conserved throughout.

options.text: The reactants total more, because some mass is used up
options.explanation: Mass is never used up in a reaction; it is rearranged into the products.

options.text: The comparison depends on the particular equation
options.explanation: Conservation applies to every balanced equation, so the totals always match.

lessons.title: Formula Masses of Larger Compounds
sourceHeadings: How to calculate relative formula mass
lessons.opening: Bigger formulas bring brackets, and brackets multiply: a subscript after a closing bracket doubles or triples every element inside. Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, holds one calcium, two oxygens and two hydrogens, while ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, holds two nitrogens, eight hydrogens, one sulfur and four oxygens. List the atoms element by element first, then total their Ar values once.
keyPoints: A subscript written after a closing bracket multiplies every element inside that bracket.
Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, contains one calcium, two oxygens and two hydrogens.
Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, contains two nitrogens, eight hydrogens, one sulfur and four oxygens.
Total larger formulae element by element: multiply each Ar by its atom count, then add the results.
Listing the atoms present before adding is the fastest guard against miscounting bracketed groups.

low.restatement: For Ca(OH)2, the bracket gives two O and two H alongside one Ca, so the total reads (1 x 40) + (2 x 16) + (2 x 1) = 74.
low.analogy: A bracketed group works like a multipack: (OH)2 buys two packs, each holding one oxygen and one hydrogen, so two of each land in the basket.
low.examPointer: Write the atoms-present list before any arithmetic; examiners award the method even when a final total slips.

medium.restatement: Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, shows the method at full size: two nitrogens, eight hydrogens, one sulfur and four oxygens give (2 x 14) + (8 x 1) + (1 x 32) + (4 x 16) = 132.
medium.analogy: Keep the receipt layout: one line per element with its count times its Ar, then a single addition at the bottom - the same discipline as the simple compounds, one row longer.
medium.examPointer: Potassium carbonate, K2CO3, is a favourite check: (2 x 39) + (1 x 12) + (3 x 16) = 138, with no brackets at all.

check.stem: How many of each atom does calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, contain?

options.text: One Ca, two O and two H
options.explanation: The bracket holds one O and one H, and the subscript 2 multiplies both.

options.text: One Ca, one O and one H
options.explanation: This ignores the subscript 2, which multiplies the whole bracket.

options.text: One Ca, one O and two H
options.explanation: The subscript 2 applies to the oxygen inside the bracket as well as the hydrogen.

options.text: Two Ca, two O and two H
options.explanation: The subscript sits outside the bracket, so it never touches the calcium.

check.stem: Using Ar values Ca = 40, O = 16 and H = 1, what is the relative formula mass of Ca(OH)2?

options.explanation: This misses the bracket doubling, counting only one O and one H.
This forgets the two hydrogens, which add 2 to the total.

check.stem: Using Ar values K = 39, C = 12 and O = 16, what is the relative formula mass of potassium carbonate, K2CO3?

options.explanation: This counts one potassium only; the subscript 2 doubles the 39.
This counts two oxygens instead of three, losing 16 from the total.
This borrows 40 as the Ar of potassium; potassium's value is 39.

check.stem: Which atom counts does ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, give?

options.text: Two N, eight H, one S and four O
options.explanation: The bracket doubles both the N and the four H inside it, then the sulfate adds S and O.

options.text: One N, four H, one S and four O
options.explanation: This reads the formula as if the bracket carried no multiplier at all.

options.text: Two N, six H, one S and four O
options.explanation: Adding the subscript instead of multiplying gives 4 + 2 hydrogens; multiplying gives 4 x 2 = 8.

options.text: One N, eight H, one S and four O
options.explanation: The subscript doubles the nitrogen inside the bracket just as it doubles the hydrogen.

check.stem: Using Ar values N = 14, H = 1, S = 32 and O = 16, what is the relative formula mass of (NH4)2SO4?

options.explanation: This ignores the bracket doubling, counting one N and four H.
This counts six hydrogens; the bracket gives 4 x 2 = 8.
This counts five oxygens; the formula shows four, contributing 64.

glossary.definition: The mass of an atom of an element compared with a standard, shown as the larger of the two numbers beside its symbol on the Periodic Table.
The total of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms present in a formula; symbol Mr.
The name for relative formula mass when the substance is a simple molecule.
As in the law of conservation of mass: mass can be neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the totals on both sides of a balanced equation match.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; their abundances fix the element's relative atomic mass.
The small number written after a symbol or bracket, giving how many of that atom the formula contains.
The plural of formula: the written patterns of symbols and subscripts that state what a substance is made of.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the relative formula mass of sodium chloride, NaCl, copper oxide, CuO, and magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO3)2. Relative atomic masses: Na 23, Cl 35.5, Cu 63.5, O 16, Mg 24, N 14.
steps: Magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO3)2, holds one Mg, two N and six O; the two nitrogens give 14 x 2 = 28.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The relative formula masses are 58.5 for sodium chloride, 79.5 for copper oxide and 148 for magnesium nitrate.
